title: Definitions of Nursing and Early Nursing Theorists
body:
## What it is
Nursing has been defined in several ways, and the exam likes to match each definition to its author. Think of them as different lenses on the same job.

## Must-know facts
- **American Nurses Association (2003):** nursing is protecting, promoting and optimizing health and abilities, preventing illness and injury, easing suffering by diagnosing and treating human responses, and advocating for individuals, families, communities and populations.
- **Florence Nightingale (1820-1910):** the first nursing theorist, called "the Lady with the Lamp". Nursing means using the **environment** of the patient to help recovery (Environmental Theory).
  - Five environmental factors: pure air, pure water, efficient drainage, cleanliness, and light (direct sunlight). Shortage of these produces illness.
  - She also stressed warmth, a quiet room and attention to diet.
- **Virginia Henderson (Nature of Nursing Model):** the unique function of the nurse is to help a sick or well person do the activities that support health, recovery or a peaceful death that they would do unaided if they had the strength, will or knowledge, and to help them regain **independence** as fast as possible.
  - Her 14 fundamental needs run from breathing, eating and drinking, eliminating, moving and positioning, sleep and rest, clothing, body temperature, hygiene, and avoiding danger, to communicating, worship, work with a sense of accomplishment, recreation, and learning.
- **Faye Abdellah (Patient-Centered Approaches):** lists 21 nursing problems and sees nursing as a service to individuals and families, an art and a science.

## How the exam asks about it
Usually "which theorist is associated with..." Anchor words: environment = Nightingale; 14 needs and independence = Henderson; 21 problems = Abdellah.

## Memory aid
Henderson = "14 needs, independence"; Abdellah = "21 problems" (just numbers to attach to names).

## Related topics
[[Nursing Theories: Johnson, King, Leininger and Levine]], [[Nursing Theories: Neuman, Orem, Peplau and Rogers]], [[Nursing Theories: Roy, Hall, Orlando, Watson and Parse]], [[Scope and Standards of Nursing Practice]]
outlineRefs: NURSING THEORIES AND CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK: Nightingale, Henderson, Abdellah

title: Nursing Theories: Johnson, King, Leininger and Levine
body:
## What it is
Four theories to match with their key words. Memorise the author plus the "signature number or term".

## Must-know facts
- **Dorothy Johnson, Behavioral System Model:** each person is a behavioral system with **7 subsystems**: ingestive, eliminative, affiliative, aggressive, dependence, achievement, and sexual/role identity. (The handout spells the first one "injective"; the usual term is ingestive.)
- **Imogene King, Goal Attainment Theory:** nursing is an interaction between nurse and patient that leads to goals being reached. The patient sits within 3 interacting systems:
  - personal/operational (the individual)
  - interpersonal (nurse-patient)
  - social (the health care system)
- **Madeleine Leininger, Transcultural Nursing (Cultural Care Diversity and Universality):** caring is universal but its expression, process and patterns differ among cultures. Three intervention modes:
  - culture care preservation/maintenance
  - culture care accommodation/negotiation
  - culture care restructuring/repatterning
- **Myra Levine, Four Conservation Principles:** conserve energy, structural integrity, personal integrity and social integrity.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which theory fits a nurse who adapts care to a client's cultural beliefs?" = Leininger. "Seven subsystems" = Johnson. "Conservation" = Levine. "Goal attainment" = King.

## Related topics
[[Definitions of Nursing and Early Nursing Theorists]], [[Nursing Theories: Neuman, Orem, Peplau and Rogers]], [[Nursing Theories: Roy, Hall, Orlando, Watson and Parse]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout names King's systems "operational, interpersonal, social"; many texts say "personal, interpersonal, social". Johnson's first subsystem is usually "ingestive".

title: Nursing Theories: Neuman, Orem, Peplau and Rogers
body:
## What it is
Four more theories commonly tested by name and key feature.

## Must-know facts
- **Betty Neuman, Health Care Systems Model:** nursing deals with all variables that affect a person's response to stress. Stressors are intrapersonal (within), interpersonal (between people) and extrapersonal (outside the person). Interventions aim to keep or restore **system stability**.
- **Dorothea Orem, Self-Care and Self-Care Deficit Theory:** self-care means the activities people do for themselves to promote and maintain well-being. Three nursing systems, chosen by how much the client can do:
  - **Wholly compensatory:** the client cannot control the environment or process information (for example, unconscious).
  - **Partly compensatory:** the client can do some but not all self-care.
  - **Supportive-educative:** the client needs to learn self-care and needs help to do so.
- **Hildegard Peplau, Psychodynamic / Interpersonal Relations:** built on the therapeutic nurse-client relationship, which passes through 4 phases: orientation, identification, exploitation, resolution.
- **Martha Rogers, Science of Unitary Human Beings:** the person is an irreducible whole, greater than the sum of the parts; a four-dimensional energy field that interacts continuously and creatively with the environment and takes part in change.

## Reasoning tip
Orem questions are about matching the nursing system to client ability: the more dependent the client, the more the nurse compensates.

## Related topics
[[Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases]], [[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Nursing Theories: Johnson, King, Leininger and Levine]], [[Nursing Theories: Roy, Hall, Orlando, Watson and Parse]]

title: Nursing Theories: Roy, Hall, Orlando, Watson and Parse
body:
## What it is
The last group of theorists in the handout. Each has a clear label.

## Must-know facts
- **Sister Callista Roy, Adaptation Model:** adaptation is the process and result of using conscious awareness and choice to create integration of the person and environment. Goal: enhance life processes through 4 adaptive modes: physiologic, self-concept, role function, interdependence.
- **Lydia Hall, Care, Core and Cure:**
  - Care = nurturing; exclusive to nursing.
  - Core = therapeutic use of self and reflection.
  - Cure = nursing related to the physician's orders.
- **Ida Jean Orlando (1961), Dynamic Nurse-Patient Relationship:** nurses give direct help to meet an immediate need and so prevent or relieve distress or helplessness. The nursing situation has 3 elements: client behavior, nurse reaction, nurse action.
- **Jean Watson (1979), Human Caring Theory:** caring is the unifying focus of practice. Ten curative (carative) factors, including:
  - humanistic-altruistic values
  - instilling faith and hope
  - sensitivity to self and others
  - a helping-trusting relationship
  - accepting expression of positive and negative feelings
  - systematic problem solving
  - transpersonal teaching-learning
  - a supportive, protective environment
  - helping with need gratification
  - allowing for existential-phenomenological-spiritual forces
- **Rosemarie Parse, Human Becoming:** three assumptions - freely choosing personal meaning, co-creating rhythmic patterns with the universe, and "contrascending" (moving beyond) with emerging possibilities while bearing responsibility for health patterns.

## Memory aid
Hall's "Care-Core-Cure" is simply the three words themselves; Roy = four modes (made-up hook: "PSRI").

## Related topics
[[Definitions of Nursing and Early Nursing Theorists]], [[Nursing Theories: Neuman, Orem, Peplau and Rogers]]

title: Scope and Standards of Nursing Practice
body:
## What it is
The scope tells what nurses do for people; the standards say how well and in what manner it must be done.

## Scope of nursing practice
- **Promoting health and wellness:** activities that raise quality of life and potential, such as better nutrition and fitness, preventing drug and alcohol misuse, limiting smoking, and preventing accidents at home and work.
- **Preventing illness:** immunizations, prenatal and infant care, prevention of sexually transmitted infections.
- **Restoring health:** care of the ill from early detection through recovery: direct care, diagnostic and assessment procedures, teaching about recovery, rehabilitation to the best functional level.
- **Caring for the dying:** helping clients live as comfortably as possible until death and helping their support people cope.

## Standards of practice
- Clinical standards follow the process: assessment, diagnosis, outcome identification, planning, implementation, evaluation.
- Professional performance standards: quality of practice, education, professional practice evaluation, collegiality, collaboration, ethics, research, resource utilization, leadership.

## How the exam asks about it
A scenario describes an activity (for example, giving a vaccine) and asks which scope area it belongs to (illness prevention). Self-evaluating your own practice against standards = professional practice evaluation.

## Related topics
[[The Nursing Process: Purposes and Characteristics]], [[Roles and Functions of the Nurse]], [[Leavell and Clark Prevention Levels with Examples]]

title: Roles and Functions of the Nurse
body:
## What it is
A nurse wears many hats. Exam items give a short action and ask which role it shows.

## Must-know facts
- **Caregiver:** helps clients physically and psychologically while keeping their dignity; primarily concerned with the client's needs.
- **Communicator:** relays the client's problems to the rest of the team.
- **Teacher:** teaches clients about their health and the procedures needed for recovery.
- **Client advocate:** protects the client; helps them use their rights and speak for themselves.
- **Counselor:** gives emotional, intellectual and psychological support.
- **Change agent:** helps clients modify behavior.
- **Leader:** influences others to work together toward a goal.
- **Manager:** plans, directs, develops staff, monitors operations, rewards fairly, and represents both staff and administration.
- **Case manager:** works with the multidisciplinary team to measure how well the case management plan works and to monitor outcomes.
- **Researcher:** takes part in scientific investigation and uses findings to improve care.
- **Collaborator:** works in combined effort with everyone involved in care.

## How the exam asks about it
- Speaking up when a client's wishes are ignored = advocate.
- Showing a diabetic how to inject insulin = teacher.
- Helping a smoker quit = change agent.

## Related topics
[[Expanded Career Roles for Nurses]], [[Scope and Standards of Nursing Practice]], [[Communication Process and Characteristics in Nursing]]
outlineRefs: ROLES AND FUNCTIONS OF A NURSE

title: Expanded Career Roles for Nurses
body:
## What it is
Advanced and specialised paths that build on the RN license.

## Must-know facts
- **Nurse practitioner:** has advanced education from an NP program; works in agencies or community settings; deals with non-emergency acute or chronic illness and gives primary ambulatory care.
- **Clinical nurse specialist:** advanced degree or expertise in a specialty (for example gerontology, oncology); gives direct care, educates others, does research and manages care.
- **Certified registered nurse anesthetist (CRNA):** advanced education in anesthesia; does pre- and post-operative visits and assessments and gives general anesthesia for surgery under supervision of a physician prepared in anesthesiology.
- **Nurse-midwife:** RN with midwifery training; gives prenatal and postnatal care and manages deliveries in normal pregnancies; may also do Pap smears, family planning and routine breast exams.
- **Nurse researcher:** studies nursing problems to improve care and expand knowledge; usually in academic institutions, teaching hospitals or research centers, often doctorate-prepared.
- **Nurse administrator:** manages client care and delivery of nursing services; functions include budgeting, staffing and program planning.
- **Nurse educator:** classroom and clinical teaching.
- **Nurse entrepreneur:** manages health-related businesses.

## Memory aid
Match the verb: practitioner = primary care, specialist = expert in one area, anesthetist = anesthesia, midwife = normal deliveries, administrator = budget and staff, educator = teach.

## Related topics
[[Roles and Functions of the Nurse]], [[Benner's Stages of Nursing Expertise]]

## Check against your textbook
Scope of these roles (especially CRNA and nurse practitioner) depends on the country's law; check Philippine regulations.

title: Benner's Stages of Nursing Expertise
body:
## What it is
Patricia Benner describes how a nurse grows from rule-follower to intuitive expert.

## The five stages
- **Stage I, Novice:** no experience (student nurse). Performance is limited and rigid, ruled by context-free rules rather than experience.
- **Stage II, Advanced beginner:** marginally acceptable performance; recognizes meaningful "aspects" of real situations and has seen enough to make some judgments.
- **Stage III, Competent:** about 2-3 years of experience; organizes and plans well, separates important from less important factors, coordinates several complex care demands.
- **Stage IV, Proficient:** about 3-5 years; sees the situation as a **whole** rather than parts, uses maxims as guides, understands the client holistically (which improves decisions) and focuses on long-term goals.
- **Stage V, Expert:** fluid, flexible, highly proficient; no longer needs rules or maxims; acts because "it felt right" (intuition).

## How the exam asks about it
A nurse who "no longer relies on rules and acts on intuition" is expert. One who "plans and organizes but is not yet seeing the whole picture" is competent. Years of experience are the easiest clue.

## Memory aid
Novice, Advanced beginner, Competent, Proficient, Expert: N-A-C-P-E (made up).

## Related topics
[[Expanded Career Roles for Nurses]], [[Roles and Functions of the Nurse]]
outlineRefs: PATRICIA BENNER'S STAGES OF NURSING EXPERTISE

title: Communication Process and Characteristics in Nursing
body:
## What it is
Communication is the exchange of ideas, information and feelings between two or more people, through words and also through gestures and body actions.

## Must-know facts
- **Verbal** communication uses spoken or written words. **Non-verbal** uses gestures, facial expression, posture and gait, body movement, appearance, eye contact and tone of voice.
- **Components:**
  - Sender: encodes and delivers the message.
  - Message: the content (verbal, non-verbal, symbolic).
  - Receiver: receives and decodes it.
  - Channel: how it travels - visual, auditory, tactile.
  - Response/feedback: what the receiver returns to the sender.
- **Characteristics of effective communication:**
  - Simplicity: commonly understood words.
  - Pace and intonation: change the feeling and impact.
  - Clarity and brevity: direct and simple.
  - Timing and relevance: right moment and fitting the client's concerns.
  - Adaptability: adjust to the client's cues.
  - Credibility: trustworthiness and reliability.
  - Humor: can help clients adjust to a painful situation.

## Exam reasoning
When words and body language disagree, trust the non-verbal message and explore it by asking the client. Use simple language, check understanding, and respond to the client's cues.

## Related topics
[[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases]], [[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]]

title: Documentation Purposes and Types of Records
body:
## What it is
Documentation is the written or computer-based permanent record of a client's information and care. It is a formal, legal document that is evidence of the care given.

## Purposes
Planning care, communication among the team, legal purposes, research, education, reimbursement, statistics/reporting/epidemiology, auditing agencies, and health care analysis.

## Types of records
- **Source-oriented medical record (SOMR, traditional):** each person or department writes in its own section of the chart, so specific information is easy to find. Components: admission sheet, face sheet, history and physical, diagnostic findings, TPR graphic sheet, doctor's order sheet, therapeutic sheet, special flow sheets, medication record, nurses' notes, discharge plan and referral summary, initial nursing assessment.
- **Problem-oriented medical record (POMR):** data are organised around the client's problems, and all team members' findings about a problem are integrated. Four parts:
  - Database: everything gathered on admission (nursing assessment, physician's history, social and family data, exam results).
  - Problem list: all aspects of life needing care; kept at the front of the chart, listed in the order identified, updated as problems resolve or appear.
  - Initial list of orders or plan of care, made by the person who lists the problem.
  - Progress notes, including narrative notes in SOAPIE or SOAPIER form.
- **Kardex:** a concise, quick-access summary of client care data for the whole team. It can be written in pencil because details change often, and is kept as flip cards in a portable file.

## Related topics
[[Rules for Charting and Recording]], [[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's first sentence for POMR ("recorded according to sources") sounds like SOMR; verify the definition.

title: Rules for Charting and Recording
body:
## What it is
General guidelines that make a chart legal, accurate and safe.

## Must-know facts
- **Date and time:** needed for legal reasons and client safety; use conventional time (9:00 am) or the 24-hour clock to avoid am/pm confusion.
- **Timing:** record as soon as possible after assessment or intervention. Never chart **before** giving care.
- **Legibility and permanence:** easy to read; dark permanent ink.
- **Terminology and spelling:** only agency-approved abbreviations, symbols and terms; look up spellings.
- **Signature:** every entry signed with name and title.
- **Accuracy:** client's name on every page; record facts and observations, not opinion. Fact: "Client refused medication." Opinion: "Client was uncooperative."
  - Correcting a mistake: draw a single line through it, write "mistaken entry" (avoid the word "error") with your initials or name. Do not erase, blot out or use correction fluid.
  - Write on every line, not between lines; draw a line through blank space and sign.
- **Sequence:** events in the order they happened.
- **Appropriateness:** only information pertaining to the client's health problems (irrelevant details can invade privacy).
- **Completeness:** include care omitted because of refusal, what and why, and who was notified.
- **Conciseness:** brief but complete.
- **Legal prudence and confidentiality:** accurate charting protects clients and staff; only professionals taking part in the care may read the chart.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which entry is correct?" Choose the objective, specific, timed, signed one; reject the vague or judgmental one. For a wrong entry choose single line + "mistaken entry" + initials.

## Related topics
[[Documentation Purposes and Types of Records]], [[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]]

title: Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders
body:
## What it is
Reporting is sharing information about client care between two or more people, face to face or by phone.

## Types of reports
- **Change-of-shift report (endorsement):** quick summary of health needs and care to be given, for continuity. It is not just reading the Kardex aloud.
- **Telephone report:** clear, accurate, concise. Include date and time, name of the person giving the information, subject, and name and signature of the receiver. The receiver **repeats it back** to confirm.
- **Transfer report:** done when moving a client to another unit.

## Telephone orders (high-yield rules)
- Only an RN may receive them.
- A second RN should listen on another line to countercheck.
- Write the date and time received.
- Write the complete order and **read it back**.
- Question the provider about any order that is unusual or contraindicated by the client's condition.
- The physician must countersign within the prescribed period (24 hours in the handout).

## Exam reasoning
Safety and verification come first: read-back, witness, then clarify odd orders before carrying them out.

## Related topics
[[Rules for Charting and Recording]], [[Communication Process and Characteristics in Nursing]]

## Check against your textbook
Rules on who may receive verbal or telephone orders and the countersigning period vary by agency and law; confirm Philippine hospital policy.

title: The Nursing Process: Purposes and Characteristics
body:
## What it is
The nursing process is a systematic, problem-solving method for giving nursing care. Its five steps spell **ADPIE**: Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation.

## Purposes
- Identify the client's health status, both actual problems and potential problems or needs.
- Establish plans to meet identified needs.
- Deliver specific nursing care and improve its quality.

## Characteristics
- **Cyclical** (repeated) and **dynamic** (always changing).
- **Client-centered:** care is organised around the client's problems, not nursing goals.
- **Problem-solving:** aimed at the client's responses to illness.
- **Decision making** in every phase.
- **Interpersonal and collaborative:** talks with client and family and works with the team.
- **Universally applicable:** any setting, any age group.
- Requires critical thinking skills.

## Exam reasoning
"What is the first step?" is almost always **assess**: gather and validate data before diagnosing or acting. Stable data first, then plan. An emergency uses ABC or Maslow to set priorities.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 1: Assessment Methods and Types]], [[Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis]], [[Nursing Process Phase 3: Planning and Goal Setting]], [[Nursing Process Phases 4 and 5: Implementation and Evaluation Types]]

title: Nursing Process Phase 1: Assessment Methods and Types
body:
## What it is
Assessment is the systematic, continuous collection, organisation, validation and documentation of data about health status. Its purpose is to build a **database**.

## Data collection
- Consider physical, psychological, emotional, sociocultural and spiritual factors.
- **Sources:** the client (primary); support people, family, friends, caregivers (secondary); client records, medical records, other therapists' records, lab records, other health professionals, literature.
- **Methods:** observing (using the senses: noticing, then selecting/organising/interpreting) and interviewing (planned conversation with a purpose).

## Interview approaches and stages
- **Directive:** structured, closed (yes/no) questions, nurse controls; used to get specific data and in emergencies.
- **Non-directive (rapport-building):** client controls subject and pace, open-ended questions; lets the client explain.
- **Stages:** opening (most important: rapport and orientation), body (client shares thoughts and feelings), closing.

## After collection
Organise (cluster facts), **validate** (double-check accuracy), and document.

## Four types of assessment
- **Initial:** within a set time after admission; creates the baseline database.
- **Problem-focused:** checks the status of a specific problem (for example hydration every 15 minutes).
- **Emergency:** during an acute crisis; find life-threatening problems using **ABC** (airway, breathing, circulation) or Maslow.
- **Time-lapsed:** months after the initial one, to compare with baseline.

## Related topics
[[The Nursing Process: Purposes and Characteristics]], [[Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

title: Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis
body:
## What it is
The second phase: analysing the data to identify the client's health care needs and write a nursing diagnosis, a statement of an actual or potential alteration in health status that nurses can treat independently.

## Activities
Cluster data, compare with norms, analyse, spot gaps and inconsistencies, then decide on problems, risks and strengths. Final output: the diagnostic statement.

## Statement formats
- **Two-part:** Problem + Etiology, joined by "related to". Example: Constipation related to prolonged laxative use.
- **Three-part (PES):** Problem, Etiology, Signs and symptoms ("as manifested by").
- **One-part:** NANDA label only, for example Rape-trauma syndrome.
- **Collaborative problems:** written as "Potential complication: ..." (for example, increased intracranial pressure after head injury).

## NANDA
Defines, refines and promotes a taxonomy of nursing diagnostic terms; members include staff nurses, clinical specialists, faculty and researchers.

## Types of nursing diagnosis
- **Actual:** present now with signs and symptoms (Ineffective breathing pattern; Anxiety).
- **Risk:** no problem yet but risk factors exist (Risk for infection).
- **Wellness:** readiness for enhancement (Readiness for enhanced family coping).
- **Possible:** evidence incomplete or unclear.
- **Syndrome:** a cluster of related diagnoses (Risk for disuse syndrome).

## Exam reasoning
A "risk" diagnosis has no "as manifested by" part, because there are no signs yet.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 1: Assessment Methods and Types]], [[Nursing Process Phase 3: Planning and Goal Setting]]

title: Nursing Process Phase 3: Planning and Goal Setting
body:
## What it is
A deliberate, systematic phase of decision making and problem solving. Goals give criteria for evaluation, so they must be written in **behavioral (measurable) terms**, and the client and family should be involved.

## Types of planning
- **Initial planning:** by the nurse who did the admission assessment.
- **Ongoing planning:** by all nurses caring for the client, e.g., at the start of each shift.
- **Discharge planning:** anticipating needs after discharge; starts at first contact and needs continuous assessment.

## The planning process
Set priorities, set client goals/outcomes, select interventions, then write individualised interventions in the care plan.

## Guidelines for writing care plans
Date and sign; use category headings; use approved symbols and key words; be specific; refer to procedure books rather than listing every step; tailor to the client's preferences; include prevention and health maintenance as well as restorative care; include ongoing assessment, collaboration and coordination, and discharge/home care needs.

## Goals: CSMART (as in the handout)
Client-centered, Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Realistic, Time-bound.

## Exam reasoning
Pick the goal with a specific observable behaviour and a time frame ("will walk 10 meters unassisted by day 3"), not a nurse-centered or vague goal ("will feel better").

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 2: Nursing Diagnosis]], [[Nursing Process Phases 4 and 5: Implementation and Evaluation Types]]
outlineRefs: Guidelines for Writing Nursing Care Plans

title: Nursing Process Phases 4 and 5: Implementation and Evaluation Types
body:
## Implementation
Doing and documenting the nursing actions that carry out the plan.
- Reassess the client **before** acting (the situation may have changed).
- Decide whether you need help.
- Perform the interventions, supervise delegated care, and document.
- Requirements: adequate knowledge, technical skills, communication skills, therapeutic use of self, right attitude.

## Evaluation
Collect and compare data, relate nursing actions to outcomes, draw conclusions about the problem's status, then **continue, modify or terminate** the care plan.

## Types of evaluation
- **Ongoing/formative:** during or right after an intervention; allows on-the-spot changes.
- **Intermittent:** at set times; shows progress and lets the nurse correct deficiencies.
- **Terminal/summative:** at or just before discharge; decides if goals were met, partly met or unmet.

## If a goal is partly or not met
Two conclusions are possible: the plan needs revising because the problem is only partly resolved, or the plan is fine and the client just needs more time.

## Exam reasoning
If the client is not improving, reassess and modify the plan; do not blame the client or stop care. Reassessment comes before any new action.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Process Phase 3: Planning and Goal Setting]], [[The Nursing Process: Purposes and Characteristics]]

title: Health and Illness Models: Travis, Health Belief and Smith
body:
## What it is
Models that explain what health means and why people act as they do.

## Definitions
- **WHO:** health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease or infirmity.
- **Walter Cannon:** health is the ability to keep homeostasis (dynamic equilibrium), regulated by negative feedback.

## Travis' Illness-Wellness Continuum
Runs from **high-level wellness to premature death**, two arrows from a neutral point. Moving toward wellness is achieved by awareness, education and growth; moving the other way means decreasing health.

## Health Belief Model (Becker, 1975)
Links belief and behavior.
- Individual perceptions: perceived susceptibility, seriousness, and threat of illness.
- Modifying factors: demographic (age, sex, race), socio-psychologic (peer pressure), structural (knowledge of the disease), and cues to action (internal like fatigue; external like mass media).

## Smith's models of health
- **Clinical:** health = absence of signs and symptoms.
- **Role performance:** health = ability to do one's work or roles.
- **Adaptive:** health is a creative process; disease is failed adaptation.
- **Eudemonistic:** health = actualising one's full potential.

## How the exam asks about it
"A client returns to work but still has a chronic disease" fits role performance. "Reads a poster and decides to get screened" = cue to action.

## Related topics
[[Agent-Host-Environment Model and Causes of Disease]], [[Stages of Illness and Risk Factors]], [[Leavell and Clark Prevention Levels with Examples]]

title: Agent-Host-Environment Model and Causes of Disease
body:
## What it is
Leavell and Clark's ecologic model: health and illness result from the interaction of three factors.
- **Agent:** any factor or stressor that can cause or lead to illness.
- **Host:** the person who may or may not be at risk.
- **Environment:** any factor outside the host that may or may not predispose to disease.

## Definitions
- **Illness:** a state in which physical, emotional, intellectual, social, developmental or spiritual functioning is lower than before.
- **Disease:** an alteration in body function causing reduced capacity or a shorter lifespan.

## Common causes of disease
- Biologic agents (microorganisms)
- Inherited genetic defects (hemophilia)
- Developmental defects (imperforate anus)
- Physical agents (hot and cold substances)
- Chemical agents (smoke emissions)
- Tissue response to injury (inflammation)
- Faulty chemical/metabolic processes (lack of iodine causes goiter)
- Emotional/physical reaction to stress (anxiety)

## Exam reasoning
Prevention works by breaking any link: kill or control the agent, strengthen the host (immunization, nutrition), or change the environment (sanitation).

## Related topics
[[Health and Illness Models: Travis, Health Belief and Smith]], [[Leavell and Clark Prevention Levels with Examples]], [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]]

title: Stages of Illness and Risk Factors
body:
## What it is
People move through predictable stages when they become ill.

## The stages
1. **Symptom experience:** the person comes to believe something is wrong - physical (feeling symptoms), cognitive (interpreting them), emotional (fear, anxiety).
2. **Assumption of the sick role:** accepts the illness, is excused from usual duties, and gets confirmation from family and friends.
3. **Medical care contact:** seeks professionals to validate that the illness is real, explain symptoms, and reassure or predict outcome.
4. **Dependent patient role:** depends on professionals; accepts or rejects suggestions, later becomes more passive and accepting; may regress to earlier behavior.
5. **Recovery or rehabilitation:** expected to give up the dependent role and resume former roles and responsibilities.

## Risk factors
Any situation, habit, environmental, physiologic or psychologic condition that raises vulnerability to illness or accident. Categories: genetic and physiological factors, age, environment, lifestyle.

## Exam reasoning
A client who refuses to do anything for himself in recovery is stuck in the dependent role; encourage graded independence while keeping safe. Reduced responsibility belongs to the sick-role stage.

## Related topics
[[Health and Illness Models: Travis, Health Belief and Smith]], [[Leavell and Clark Prevention Levels with Examples]]

title: Leavell and Clark Prevention Levels with Examples
body:
## What it is
Three levels of prevention, matched to the stage of disease. For community-level programs, also see [[Three Levels of Prevention]].

## Must-know facts
- **Primary prevention:** promote optimal health and raise resistance before disease exists (pre-pathologic stage). Includes health promotion and specific protection. Examples: quit smoking, limit alcohol, exercise regularly, balanced diet, lower fat and more fiber.
- **Secondary prevention (health maintenance):** find a disease early and treat promptly to limit disability. Examples: annual physical exam, regular Pap smear, monthly breast self-examination.
- **Tertiary prevention:** after disease or disability has occurred and recovery has begun; aims to stop further damage and reach the best possible health. This is **rehabilitation**. Examples: self-monitoring of blood glucose in diabetes, physical therapy after stroke, speech therapy after laryngectomy.

## How the exam asks about it
Ask "has disease already started?" No = primary. Yes, and we are screening or catching early = secondary. Yes, and we are limiting damage or rehabilitating = tertiary.

## Related topics
[[Levels of Prevention]], [[Scope and Standards of Nursing Practice]], [[Agent-Host-Environment Model and Causes of Disease]]
outlineRefs: LEAVELL AND CLARK'S THREE LEVEL OF PREVENTION

title: Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome
body:
## What it is
Stress is a universal condition in which a person responds to a change in their usual balanced state. A **stressor** is any event or stimulus that causes stress; responses are coping strategies or mechanisms.

## Sources of stress
- Internal (from within, e.g., depression in a cancer patient)
- External (outside, e.g., a death in the family)
- Developmental (predictable life stages, e.g., starting a career)
- Situational (unpredictable, positive or negative, e.g., marriage, divorce, birth of a child)

## Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)
The whole body responds; many diseases share the same general signs.
- **Alarm reaction:** body defenses alerted, person aware of threat, resistance temporarily lowered, adaptive mechanisms mobilised. Very intense stress can cause death even here.
  - Shock phase: autonomic nervous system reacts, large amounts of epinephrine and cortisol released, "fight or flight", lasts about 1 minute to 24 hours.
  - Countershock phase: shock changes are reversed.
- **Stage of resistance:** adaptation happens; the body tries to confine the stressor to the smallest area and returns toward homeostasis.
- **Stage of exhaustion:** coping has run out; effects may spread to the whole body, ending in recovery after rest or, at worst, death.
- **Local Adaptation Syndrome (LAS):** one organ or body part responds (inflammation, backache, headache, diarrhea).

## Exam reasoning
Sequence: alarm, resistance, exhaustion. "Fight or flight" = alarm/shock.

## Related topics
[[Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response]], [[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]], [[Anxiety and Anxiety Disorders]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout labels cortisone; the stress hormone is cortisol. Its layout of alarm substages is muddled; check the standard order.
outlineRefs: PHYSIOLOGIC RESPONSES TO STRESS AND ILLNESS
RESPONSE BASED MODEL OF STRESS (HANS SELYE)

title: Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response
body:
## Homeostasis
A state of dynamic equilibrium (balance, stability), maintained by **negative feedback**. Walter Cannon's concepts include the sympatho-adreno-medullary response (fight or flight), adreno-cortical response and neurohypophyseal response.

## Inflammation
A local response to tissue injury or infection that mobilises specific and non-specific defenses. Purposes: localise the injury, protect tissue from further injury, prepare tissue for repair.

## Cellular response
- **Neutrophils** arrive first.
- **Monocytes** perform phagocytosis in chronic injury.
- **Lymphocytes** handle immune responses.

## Processes
- Margination/pavementing: phagocytes line up along vessel walls.
- Emigration/diapedesis: phagocytes move out of vessels.
- Chemotaxis: injured tissue releases substances that attract phagocytes.
- Phagocytosis: phagocytes engulf antigens.

## Exudate
Fluid that escaped the vessels plus dead phagocytes and tissue cells. Fibrinogen (becoming fibrin), thromboplastin from injured cells, and platelets form a mesh that walls off the area and stops spread. When the agent is overcome, lymphatic drainage clears the exudate.

## Memory aid
Order of events: Margination, Emigration, Chemotaxis, Phagocytosis (MECP, made up).

## Related topics
[[Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions]], [[Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says homeostasis is more commonly called "hemodynamics"; the usual term is homeodynamics (hemodynamics means blood flow). Verify.

title: Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions
body:
## What it is
The reparative phase after inflammation.

## Two ways tissue repairs
- **Regeneration:** damaged cells replaced by new cells identical in structure and function.
- **Scar formation:** damaged cells replaced by fibrous tissue.
  - Granulation tissue: early stage; pink or red, fragile, gelatinous.
  - Cicatrix (scar): later stage; tissue shrinks as collagen fibers contract.

## Healing by intention
- **First intention:** clean-cut wound with edges approximated; minimal or no scar (surgical incision).
- **Second intention:** extensive wound with much tissue loss; edges not joined, longer repair, greater scarring.
- **Third intention:** delayed surgical closure of an infected wound (closed after infection is controlled).

## How the exam asks about it
Match the wound: sutured clean incision = first; large open pressure ulcer = second; contaminated wound left open then closed days later = third.

## Related topics
[[Homeostasis and the Inflammatory Response]], [[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]]

title: Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia
body:
## What it is
Temperature is the balance between heat produced and heat lost. Vital (cardinal) signs: temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, plus pain as the fifth.

## Types
- **Core:** deep tissues (abdominal and pelvic cavity).
- **Surface:** skin, subcutaneous tissue and fat; rises and falls with the environment.

## Heat loss
- Radiation: surface to surface without contact.
- Conduction: direct contact.
- Convection: air currents.
- Evaporation: moisture vaporising from respiratory tract, mouth and skin.

## Factors affecting temperature
Age, circadian rhythm (highest about 4-6 pm, lowest about 4-6 am), exercise, hormones (progesterone raises it), stress, environment.

## Alterations
- **Pyrexia/fever:** above usual range. **Hyperpyrexia:** 41 C (105.8 F) and above.
- **Hypothermia:** core temperature below normal; from excess heat loss, poor heat production or impaired hypothalamic regulation.

## Fever patterns
- Intermittent: alternates regularly between fever and normal/subnormal.
- Remittent: wide fluctuations (over 2 C in 24 h), always above normal.
- Relapsing: a few febrile days then 1-2 normal days.
- Constant: minimal change, stays above normal.
- Spike: rapid rise then return to normal within hours.

## Related topics
[[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]], [[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]], [[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]]

title: Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales
body:
## Oral
Most convenient. Wait 30 minutes after hot/cold drinks, food or smoking. Avoid in oral lesions or surgery, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, oronasal pack, NGT or ET tube, seizure-prone, very young, unconscious, restless or confused clients. Place the bulb beside the frenulum for 2-3 minutes. Normal 36-37.5 C.

## Rectal
Very accurate. Avoid with anal/rectal conditions or surgery, diarrhea, quadriplegia and myocardial infarction. Use gloves, Sim's (lateral) position, lubricate, ask the client to breathe slowly, never force. Hold 2 minutes. Normal 36-37.8 C.

## Axillary
Safest and non-invasive. Pat the axilla dry (rubbing raises skin temperature), bulb in the center, arm tight across chest, leave about 9 minutes.

## Tympanic
Common estimate of core temperature. Adults: pull pinna back and up. Children under 3: pull straight back and slightly down. Over 3: back and up. Aim toward the eardrum, insert snugly with a circular motion.

## Conversions
- F to C: 5/9 x (F - 32)
- C to F: (C x 9/5) + 32

## Exam reasoning
Pick the site that is safe for the client's condition: axillary for the very young or confused, not oral.

## Related topics
[[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]], [[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout gives rectal insertion as 15 cm (6 in) in adults and 11 cm in children; standard texts say about 3-4 cm (1.5 in) for adults. Axillary time of 9 minutes and the quoted normal ranges should also be verified.

title: Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever
body:
## What it is
A cooling measure using lukewarm water to bring down a raised temperature.

## Must-know facts
- Start when body temperature rises 1-2 C.
- Water temperature in the handout: 32 C.
- Apply by **patting**, not rubbing. Rationale: friction creates heat and raises temperature.
- Do **not** use alcohol. Rationale: it dries and irritates the skin.

## Nursing considerations
Prevent chilling and shivering (shivering produces heat), check temperature afterwards, and stop if the client shivers or becomes uncomfortable. Treat the cause and give antipyretics as ordered.

## How the exam asks about it
The classic trap is the choice with alcohol or vigorous rubbing; reject it. Cold water or ice baths are also poor choices.

## Related topics
[[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]], [[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout gives only the start criterion and 32 C; the shivering advice is standard teaching I added.

title: Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics
body:
## What it is
The pulse is the wave of blood created by left ventricular contraction. Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate; normal about 5 L per minute.

## Factors affecting pulse
Age, gender (male lower than female), exercise, fever, medications, hypovolemia, stress, position change, pathology.

## Pulse sites and uses
- Temporal: when radial is not accessible.
- Carotid: cardiac arrest (adults).
- Radial: readily accessible, routine.
- Apical: routine for infants and children up to 3 years.
- Brachial: BP measurement; cardiac arrest in infants.
- Femoral: cardiac arrest/shock, leg circulation.
- Popliteal: lower leg circulation.
- Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis: circulation to the foot.

## What to assess
- Rate: adult 60-100/min; tachycardia over 100; bradycardia under 60.
- Rhythm: irregular = dysrhythmia/arrhythmia.
- Volume: normal felt with moderate pressure; full bounding is hard to obliterate; weak/thready is easily obliterated.
- Arterial wall: straight, smooth, soft, pliable.
- **Pulse deficit:** difference between apical and radial rates.
- Scale: 0 absent, 1+ weak/thready, 2+ normal, 3+ bounding.

## Related topics
[[Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms]], [[Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement]], [[Body Temperature: Heat Loss, Fever and Hypothermia]]

title: Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms
body:
## Three processes
- **Ventilation:** air moving in and out (inhalation, exhalation).
- **Diffusion:** gas exchange from higher to lower pressure at the alveolocapillary membrane.
- **Perfusion:** blood available to carry gases, nutrients and wastes.

## Control and types
- Costal (thoracic) breathing uses intercostal and accessory muscles; diaphragmatic (abdominal) uses the diaphragm.
- Medulla oblongata is the primary respiratory center; CO2 is the main chemical stimulus.
- Pons: pneumotaxic center (rhythm) and apneustic center (deep prolonged inspiration).
- Carotid and aortic bodies: chemoreceptors sensitive to O2 and CO2.

## Assessment
Normal rate 12-20/min; note depth (normal, deep, shallow), rhythm, and quality/effort and sound. Rate is affected by exercise, stress, environment, altitude and medications.

## Terms
- Tachypnea: fast shallow (over 20). Bradypnea: slow (under 12). Apnea: none.
- Hyperventilation: rapid deep. Hypoventilation: shallow.
- Cheyne-Stokes: deep to shallow then apnea. Kussmaul: rapid, deep, labored. Biot: shallow breaths interrupted by apnea.
- Dyspnea: difficult breathing. Orthopnea: breathes only when upright.
- Stridor: harsh high sound on inspiration. Stertor: snoring. Wheeze: high musical sound on expiration. Bubbling: gurgling through secretions.

## Related topics
[[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Airway Obstruction and Choking]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout defines tachypnea as "quick, shallow"; hyperventilation as rapid and deep. Confirm definitions with your text.

title: Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement
body:
## Definitions
BP is pressure of blood against arterial walls. Systolic = ventricular contraction; diastolic = ventricles at rest; pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic. Hypertension is persistently high; hypotension low; orthostatic hypotension is a drop on sitting or standing.

## Determinants
Pumping action of the heart (weak = lower BP), peripheral vascular resistance, vessel diameter (vasoconstriction raises BP), blood volume (loss lowers BP), blood viscosity (thicker raises BP).

## Other factors
Age, gender, exercise, medications, stress, obesity, race, diurnal variation, disease.

## Classification (handout)
- Normal: under 120 and under 80
- Prehypertension: 120-139 or 80-89
- Stage 1: 140-159 or 90-99
- Stage 2: 160 or more, or 100 or more

## Korotkoff sounds
Phase 1 first faint tapping; 2 swishing; 3 crisper, louder; 4 muffled blowing; 5 silence.

## Technique
Correct cuff size; client rested (wait 30 minutes after exercise, smoking, caffeine); arm at heart level, supported; cuff 1 inch above the antecubital space; palpate first, then auscultate; inflate 30 mmHg above where the pulse disappeared; deflate 2-3 mmHg per second; wait 1-2 minutes before repeating.

## Errors
- False **low**: cuff bladder too wide; arm above heart level.
- False **high**: cuff too narrow or loose; arm below heart level or unsupported; insufficient rest.

## Related topics
[[Pulse Assessment: Sites and Characteristics]], [[Pain Assessment: Types, PQRST and Scales]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's stage 2 reads ">160 or >100"; current guidance usually uses 160 or above. The classification system (older JNC 7) may differ from your textbook.

title: Pain Assessment: Types, PQRST and Scales
body:
## What it is
Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience tied to actual or potential tissue damage. It is called the "fifth vital sign" (American Pain Society, 2003). Self-report is the best evidence of pain.

## Types
- Acute: seconds up to 6 months.
- Chronic: constant or intermittent, lasting 6 months or longer (persistent, non-malignant).
- Cancer-related pain.

## Characteristics: PQRST
- Provoking factors: what were you doing at onset?
- Quality: throbbing, burning, aching, stabbing.
- Radiation: where is it, does it spread? Referred pain radiates to other areas.
- Severity: rated on a scale, 0-10.
- Time: how long, acute or chronic.

## Scales
- Descriptive intensity scale: no pain to worst possible.
- Numeric scale: 0 to 10.
- Visual analogue scale: no pain to pain as bad as it could be.
- Faces scale: suitable for children.

## Exam reasoning
Assess pain before and after intervention; believe the client's report; use a faces scale for children.

## Related topics
[[Blood Pressure: Determinants, Classification and Measurement]], [[Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy]]

title: Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy
body:
## General rules
- Head-to-toe (cephalocaudal). Check the client's level of awareness first.
- Most important consideration: prepare the client physically and psychologically.
- Protect privacy; get equipment ready beforehand.

## Techniques (IPPA)
Inspection (sight), Palpation (touch with finger pads), Percussion (tapping to produce sound), Auscultation (stethoscope). Light palpation precedes deep palpation.

## Abdomen: IAPePa
Inspection, Auscultation, Percussion, Palpation. Auscultate before touching so bowel sounds are not altered.

## Special considerations
- Palpate the painful quadrant last.
- No abdominal palpation if tumor of the liver or kidneys.
- Flex the knees to relax abdominal muscles.
- Quadrant order in the handout: right lower, right upper, left upper, left lower.
- Best position for the chest: sitting upright; for the back: standing.
- Palpate neck nodes or thyroid from behind the client.
- Darken the room for ophthalmoscopy.
- A male examiner with a female client needs a female attendant.

## Related topics
[[Percussion Sounds and Normal Breath Sounds]], [[Examination Positions]]

## Check against your textbook
Verify the quadrant sequence; many texts start in the right lower quadrant and move clockwise, which matches the handout.

title: Percussion Sounds and Normal Breath Sounds
body:
## Percussion sounds
- Flatness: soft, extremely dull; muscle and bone.
- Dullness: medium, thud-like; liver and heart.
- Resonance: loud, hollow; normal lung.
- Hyperresonance: very loud, booming; emphysematous lung.
- Tympany: loud, musical; gas-filled stomach.

## Normal breath sounds
- Vesicular: soft, low-pitched "gentle sighing" over small airways (bronchioles and alveoli).
- Bronchovesicular: moderate "blowing" over larger bronchi.
- Bronchial (tubular): high-pitched, loud, harsh over the trachea.

## How the exam asks about it
Match sound to place: hyperresonance with air trapping (emphysema), tympany with a gas-filled stomach, dullness with liver. Finding bronchial sounds over the periphery of the lung would be abnormal.

## Memory aid
Going from solid to air: flat, dull, resonant, hyperresonant, tympanic.

## Related topics
[[Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy]], [[Respiration Assessment and Abnormal Breathing Terms]]

title: Examination Positions
body:
## Positions and what they examine
- **Dorsal recumbent:** back-lying, knees flexed, hips externally rotated. Head and neck, axillae, anterior thorax, lungs, breasts, heart, abdomen, extremities, peripheral pulses, vital signs, vagina.
- **Dorsal (supine):** back-lying, legs extended. Head and neck, axilla, anterior thorax, lungs, breasts, heart, extremities, pulses.
- **Sitting:** seated, back unsupported, legs hanging. Head and neck, axillae, anterior and posterior thorax, lungs, breasts, heart, vital signs, extremities, reflexes.
- **Lithotomy:** back-lying, feet in stirrups, hips at the table edge. Female genitals, rectum, reproductive tract.
- **Sims:** side-lying, lower arm behind the body, upper leg flexed. Rectum and vagina (also used for rectal temperature).
- **Prone:** face-lying, with or without small pillow. Posterior thorax.

## Exam reasoning
Choose the position that gives access to the area and keeps the client comfortable and covered; drape for privacy.

## Related topics
[[Physical Examination: Techniques, Sequence and Privacy]], [[Measuring Temperature by Site and Converting Scales]]

title: Common Skin Problems and Skin Lesion Types
body:
## Common skin problems
- Abrasion: superficial layers scraped away; red or weeping; keep clean and dry.
- Excessive dryness: scaly, rough; increase oral fluids, moisturise, avoid alcohol.
- Acne: inflammation around sebaceous glands; avoid high-fat foods, reduce stress, do not squeeze pimples.
- Erythema: redness (rash, sun, fever); wash well, antiseptic lotion for itching.
- Hyperhidrosis: excessive sweating. Bromhidrosis: foul-smelling sweat.
- Vitiligo: hypopigmented patches from loss of melanocytes.

## Primary lesions
- Macule: flat, under 1 cm (freckle). Patch: over 1 cm (port-wine mark).
- Papule: raised, under 0.5 cm (nevus, acne). Plaque: larger than a papule.
- Nodule: solid mass into the dermis. Tumor: larger than a nodule.
- Vesicle: fluid-filled, under 1 cm (chickenpox). Bulla: large fluid-filled sac.
- Pustule: filled with pus. Wheal: localised edema. Cyst: thick-walled, fluid or semisolid.
- Telangiectasia: dilated capillaries. Petechiae: pinpoint red spots.

## Secondary lesions
Scale, crust (dried serum or pus), erosion (epidermis lost), excoriation (scratch), atrophy (thinned skin), scar, ulcer (excavation into dermis or deeper).

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook
Size cut-offs differ between textbooks (for example vesicle 0.5 vs 1 cm, plaque 0.5 vs 1 cm).

title: Bed Bath Guidelines
body:
## Purposes
Remove microorganisms, secretions and dead skin; improve circulation; promote relaxation, comfort and self-esteem; prevent odor; assess skin and body; provide activity and exercise.

## Guidelines
- Explain, provide privacy, turn off fans or air conditioning to prevent chilling.
- Offer toileting first; bed flat if allowed; client to one side.
- Cover with a bath blanket; use a bath mitt.
- Warm water, about 110-115 F (43-46 C); test with the inner wrist or elbow area and change when cooled.
- Order: eyes, face, ears, neck; far arm; near arm; hands; chest and abdomen; far leg; near leg; feet; back and buttocks; perineum last.
- Wash, rinse and dry one part at a time; rinse soap well; apply lotion; change gown and linen; clean equipment; document.

## Special points
- Eyes: clean with water only, inner to outer canthus, a separate part of the mitt for each eye.
- Limbs: long firm strokes from **distal to proximal** to promote venous return.

## Why this order
Cleanest areas first and perineum last prevents spreading microorganisms.

## Related topics
[[Tepid Sponge Bath for Fever]], [[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout uses "dorsal part of the hand or elbow" for water testing; many texts say inner wrist.
outlineRefs: Considerations when bathing a client in bed

title: Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages
body:
## What it is
A lesion caused by unrelieved pressure that damages underlying tissue.

## Risk factors
Friction and shearing, immobility, poor nutrition, fecal and urinary incontinence, decreased mental status, diminished sensation, excessive body heat, advanced age, chronic illness.

## Stages
- **Stage I:** non-blanchable redness of intact skin.
- **Stage II:** partial-thickness loss (epidermis, maybe dermis): abrasion, blister or shallow crater.
- **Stage III:** full-thickness loss with damage or necrosis of subcutaneous tissue, deep crater, not through fascia.
- **Stage IV:** full-thickness loss with extensive destruction, necrosis, or damage to muscle, bone, tendon or joint capsule.

## Exam reasoning
Stage by the deepest tissue seen: intact red = I, blister = II, fat = III, muscle or bone = IV. Black eschar cannot be staged until removed.

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment]], [[Wound Healing: Regeneration, Scar and Intentions]], [[Common Skin Problems and Skin Lesion Types]]

## Check against your textbook
The eschar staging remark is standard teaching I added; it is not in the handout.

title: Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Treatment
body:
## Prevention
- Balanced nutrition with enough protein and vitamins A, B, C and zinc; at least 2500 ml fluids a day unless contraindicated.
- Smooth, firm, wrinkle-free bed surface.
- Keep head of bed no higher than 30 degrees to reduce shearing.
- No baby powder or cornstarch; moisturise dry skin; use alcohol-free barrier films or transparent dressings.
- No massage over bony prominences.
- Reposition every 15 minutes to 2 hours depending on risk (handout range).
- Lift with a trapeze or devices rather than dragging.
- Keep skin clean and dry; assess regularly for early signs.

## Treatment
- Minimise pressure on the ulcer.
- Clean with each dressing change (hydrocolloid dressings in the handout); use surgical asepsis.
- Send drainage for culture and sensitivity.
- Cleanse gently with alcohol-free cleanser; do not use hydrogen peroxide.
- Black (necrotic) wounds need debridement:
  - sharp: scalpel
  - mechanical: moist-to-moist dressing
  - chemical: collagenase enzymes
  - autolytic: moisture-retaining dressings

## Exam reasoning
Relieve pressure first. Early prevention beats treatment.

## Related topics
[[Pressure Ulcer Risk Factors and Stages]], [[Bed Bath Guidelines]]

## Check against your textbook
The 2-hour turning interval and exact fluid and dressing choices should be checked; mechanical debridement is usually wet-to-dry.

title: Medication Administration: Ten Rights and Drug Orders
body:
## Before giving a drug
Know dose, route, actions, expected effect, interactions and adverse effects; follow agency procedure; check the order is complete (client name, date, drug, dose, route, time, signature); compare it with the medication administration record (MAR); discuss the drug with the client and recheck the order if the client disagrees.

## Ten rights
Right drug, dose, client, route, time, documentation, approach, right to know about the drug, right to refuse, right drug history.

## Routes
Oral (absorbed in the GI tract), topical (skin or mucosa), parenteral (injection); also eye, ear and suppository. Schedules: regular, one-time, as needed.

## Essential parts of a drug order
Full name of client, date and time written, drug name, dose, frequency, route, signature of the writer.

## Drug effects
- Therapeutic: intended effect.
- Side effect: secondary, predictable, may be harmless or harmful.
- Adverse: severe, may require stopping the drug.
- Toxic: overdose or buildup from impaired metabolism or excretion.
- Idiosyncratic: unexpected, individual.
- Allergic: immunologic.

## Exam reasoning
Verify the order and the client identity first; when something looks wrong, hold the drug and clarify.

## Related topics
[[Nursing Reports and Telephone Orders]], [[Rules for Charting and Recording]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout section on types of medication orders is empty in this slice; the usual five rights are expanded here to ten as listed.
